title: The Grammar a Language Model Reasons With
content: Human languages share a proto-grammar of things, actions, states and relationships: STAR (States, Things, Actions, Relationships). We ask whether large language models reason with it. A grammar does not change with what is expressed, so we probe it with problems that demand different expressions: water-jug problems posed in declared worlds whose answer key is exact, varied in scale, in physics, in whether water once measured can be taken back, in reasoning budget and in the language of the prompt. We read the reasoning of Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonnet 5 and, from their raw chains of thought, two open-weight models, gpt-oss-20b and Qwen3-30B-A3B. In every trace we coded, across probes, models and languages, the categories are those of human language; what varies is usage, such as writing a small state space as a list and a large one as a rule. The grammar also locates errors: nearly every wrong answer falls in one category, and when a translation shifts one word, the errors move into the category it touches: Relationship for a rule the Chinese wording narrowed, Thing for a capacity read as contents in French.
